passage: I'm Rafiq. My sister Jahnavi is in class 11, and for a month someone had been sending her awful messages from different accounts. She tried to handle it alone. One night I saw her crying over her phone, and I said, "Don't delete anything. Screenshot everything." We sat on the floor and saved every message into a folder, with dates. The next morning she took them to the school counsellor. I waited outside. When she came out, her face was different, lighter. She said the counsellor listened to all of it, told her it wasn't her fault, and called our parents that same afternoon. Nobody made her change classes or give up her phone. The school acted on the boys instead.

qa.q: What did Rafiq tell Jahnavi not to do?
qa.a: Rafiq told her not to delete anything and to screenshot everything.

qa.q: How can you tell Jahnavi felt relieved after meeting the counsellor?
qa.a: Her face looked different and lighter when she came out, after being believed and told it wasn't her fault.

qa.q: What made this report work well?
qa.a: Saving dated evidence made the problem clear, and the counsellor took it seriously, told her parents the same day and acted on the senders without punishing Jahnavi.

qa.q: How was Rafiq affected by watching his sister go through this?
qa.a: Rafiq was worried seeing her cry, and then likely relieved and proud as she came out looking lighter.

grounding: It shows an ally helping save screenshots, the target telling a counsellor who takes it seriously and acts without making her pay for speaking.

passage:
Tuesday. Simran showed Maria the fake posts about her. Maria's first words were, "Don't reply. Let's save them." They screenshotted each one, with dates, into a folder.
Thursday. After school, with Maria beside her, Simran knocked on Mrs D'Souza's door. Her hands were shaking. Mrs D'Souza closed the door, listened without interrupting, and said, "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault." She called Simran's father before Simran reached home.
The following Monday. Simran was still in her usual seat, with her phone, and no one had asked her to stay home. The posts were gone. In the corridor she passed Maria and smiled, a real one this time.

qa.q: Who did Simran knock on the door of on Thursday?
qa.a: She knocked on Mrs D'Souza's door.

qa.q: What does Simran's real smile on Monday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels safer and relieved, now that she was believed and the posts are gone.

qa.q: What did the adults do right after Simran reported it?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza listened, said it was not her fault, called her father the same day and acted without taking away Simran's seat or phone.

qa.q: How might Maria feel about the part Maria played?
qa.a: Maria likely feels glad and proud that helping save the evidence and staying beside Simran made a real difference. 😊

grounding: It illustrates a target and ally saving screenshots and telling a teacher who takes it seriously, without the target paying for speaking up.

passage:
Uday, you did right to tell me about those messages. Now let your Darshan chacha tell you something from when I was in Class 11.

A group of boys kept sending me cruel messages every night. I was ashamed. I thought telling would make me look weak. I deleted everything so nobody would see.

Then one night my friend Irfan said, "Stop deleting. Save them." We screenshotted every message, with dates. Twenty-three of them. And the next morning, Irfan and I took them to our counsellor, Mrs Bhatt.

She didn't say, "Just ignore them." She read every one. She called the boys' parents that week, and she made sure nobody moved me out of my section or my bench. I wasn't the one who paid.

That was the turning point: saving the proof and telling someone who took it seriously.

So tonight, we save yours. Tomorrow I'll come with you to your principal.

qa.q: How many messages did Darshan and Irfan screenshot?
qa.a: Twenty-three.

qa.q: Why had young Darshan been deleting the messages?
qa.a: He was ashamed and believed telling would make him look weak.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Darshan chacha's story?
qa.a: Saving the messages as proof and taking them to Mrs Bhatt, who took it seriously and acted without making Darshan pay.

qa.q: How did Mrs Bhatt make sure the target did not pay for speaking up?
qa.a: She called the boys' parents and made sure Darshan wasn't moved out of his section or bench.

grounding: Darshan chacha recalls saving screenshots and telling a counsellor who took it seriously, showing reporting as protection, and promises to help Uday the same way.

passage:
Vaibhav's phone was at four percent, the board exam was in two days, and the messages wouldn't stop. A fake account had been posting edited photos of him all evening.

He wanted to delete everything and throw the phone in a drawer.

His friend Sarika, video-calling from her own room, said, "Don't delete anything. Screenshot. Now, before your phone dies."

He did, fast: eleven screenshots. Then he plugged in and she made him email them to himself, and to her.

"Now tell your mother," Sarika said. "Tonight."

"She's stressed about my exam. I don't want to make it worse."

"This is making it worse. Telling isn't weak, Vaibhav. It's how you protect yourself."

He went downstairs. His mother read every screenshot. She said, "Thank you for showing me," and emailed his class teacher that night. The next morning the school reported the account and called in the students involved, without moving Vaibhav's exam seat.

qa.q: How many screenshots did Vaibhav take?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why was Vaibhav reluctant to tell his mother?
qa.a: He felt worried about adding to her exam stress and wanted to make the problem disappear by deleting it.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that turned this into protection?
qa.a: She got Vaibhav to save the evidence before his phone died and pushed him to tell his mother that same night.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's mother respond?
qa.a: She thanked him, read everything and emailed his class teacher that night.

grounding: Under exam pressure and a dying phone, Sarika helps Vaibhav save evidence and tell his mother, who takes it seriously and involves the school.

passage:
Santosh sat at the dining table in their Nagpur flat and slid his phone across to his father, Harish.

"I saved them," he said. "Screenshots. From the group. For three weeks."

Harish scrolled. His face tightened. There were photos of Santosh with insults typed over them, and voice notes mocking him.

"Why didn't you tell me earlier?"

"I thought you'd say I was weak. Or that I should hit back."

Harish put the phone down. "Telling me is not weak. It's the smart thing. Thank you."

The next morning Harish went with Santosh to meet the principal and showed her everything. She listened, kept copies, and called in the students' parents that week. When one teacher suggested moving Santosh to another section "to avoid trouble," the principal said no: "He did nothing wrong. They're the ones who'll change."

qa.q: How long had Santosh been saving screenshots?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why hadn't Santosh told his father earlier?
qa.a: He was afraid his father would call him weak or tell him to hit back.

qa.q: What did the principal do right?
qa.a: She listened, kept copies, called in the students' parents, and refused to move Santosh, so he did not pay for speaking up.

qa.q: How did Harish react when he saw the screenshots?
qa.a: His face tightened with worry and anger, but he calmly told Santosh that telling was smart, not weak, and thanked him.

grounding: Santosh saves screenshots and tells his father, who takes it seriously; the principal acts without making the target pay for reporting.

passage:
"Pradeep Sir, can I show you something?" Parul held out her phone. "I saved everything. Twenty-three screenshots, with dates."
"Sit down, Parul. Take your time."
"It's the Class 10 group. They made a page about me. My mum said I should bring these to you."
He scrolled slowly, not smiling, not rushing. "You did exactly the right thing, saving these and telling us. That isn't weakness. It's how we protect you."
"Will they know I told? Will I have to change sections?"
"No. You're not the one who moves. And your phone stays yours. I'll speak to the principal today, and the students responsible will be dealt with under the school rules."
"And if it gets worse after?"
"Then you come straight back here, any day. I'll also call your mum this afternoon so she knows what we're doing."
Parul let out a long breath. "Okay."

qa.q: How many screenshots had Parul saved?
qa.a: Twenty-three screenshots, with dates.

qa.q: What was Parul worried about as she showed the screenshots?
qa.a: She was anxious that the others would know she had told, and afraid she might be the one made to change sections.

qa.q: How did Pradeep Sir make sure Parul did not pay for speaking up?
qa.a: He said she would not move sections and her phone stays hers, that the students responsible would face the school rules, and that he would call her mum that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Parul's mum feel when Pradeep Sir calls?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and reassured that her advice was right and that the school is acting seriously.

grounding: Shows a teen saving screenshots and reporting bullying to a counsellor who takes it seriously and acts without making her pay for speaking.
